 Hydrostatic Pressure Formula: P = ρgh, Gauge and Absolute Pressure, Specific Gravity, mmWC and mbar, Tank Bottom Pressure and Transmitter Below Tap Correction

 The pressure at the bottom of any liquid column depends only on density, gravity and height. Learn how to use that rule for tank levels, transmitter ranges and mounting offsets with solved examples and a free calculator.

 
 P = ρgh 
 Gauge vs Absolute 
 Specific Gravity 
 mmWC and mbar 
 Calculator 
 




 The hydrostatic pressure formula tells you how much pressure a liquid column creates at any depth. We use it for tank bottom pressure, specific gravity, unit conversion and transmitter mounting corrections.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn the hydrostatic pressure formula P = ρgh with gauge and absolute pressure, specific gravity, level transmitter offsets and solved examples.


 
 
 

 What Is the Hydrostatic Pressure Formula?

 The hydrostatic pressure formula is P = ρ × g × h, where ρ is the liquid density, g is the acceleration due to gravity and h is the vertical height of liquid above the point. It gives the gauge pressure created by a still liquid column, and adding atmospheric pressure turns it into absolute pressure.

 Quick Answer
 P = ρ × g × h gives pressure in pascal when ρ is in kg/m³, g in m/s² and h in m
 Standard gravity is 9.80665 m/s², so 1 m of water at SG 1.0 gives 9.807 kPa or 98.07 mbar
 In plant units, P (mbar) = 98.0665 × SG × h (m)
 Absolute pressure = gauge pressure + atmospheric pressure, about 1013.25 mbar at sea level
 Pressure depends on vertical height only, not on the tank shape or volume
 

 This is the principle behind hydrostatic level measurement , where a pressure sensor at the bottom of a tank reads the liquid column above it. WIKA describes the same idea in its white paper on submersible sensors, where level is found from h = p ÷ (ρ × g).

 
 
 Image credit: WIKA . Image courtesy of WIKA, shown here for educational reference. 
 

 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 Hydrostatic Pressure Formula P = ρgh in Detail

 Think of a column of liquid with a base area A and height h. Its weight is ρ × A × h × g, and dividing that weight by the area A leaves P = ρ × g × h, so the area cancels out completely.

 
P = ρ × g × h
ρ = density, kg/m³
g = 9.80665 m/s²
h = height of liquid above the point, m
 P in Pa (N/m²) 


 In the hydrostatic pressure formula the height h is always the vertical distance from the free surface down to the point of measurement. A long sloping pipe or a wide tank does not change the answer, which is why the basics of pressure measurement always speak of head rather than volume.

 Do You Know?
 A tall thin pipe and a huge storage tank filled to the same height give exactly the same bottom pressure. This is called the hydrostatic paradox, and it was demonstrated by Blaise Pascal with a long tube fitted to a barrel.
